linq.title: LINQ for Java · PiscesCup
linq.description: LINQ for Java: an Enumerable query library for Java 25, featuring fluent queries, deferred execution and primitive-specialized sequences.
linq.lead: Composable data processing for Java collections and sequences using a LINQ query style.
linq.overview: LINQ for Java provides queries for Java collections and sequences through the Enumerable model. Methods such as where, select and orderBy compose data processing steps; many intermediate operations use deferred execution and run when results are enumerated or consumed.
linq.enumerablesIntro: Object sequences and specialized int, long and double sequences provide query entry points for the corresponding data types.
linq.objectDescription: Create sequences from arrays, collections or varargs, then filter, order, group and join objects.
linq.intDescription: Use Linq.ofInts for int-specific queries and numeric aggregation such as sum and average.
linq.longDescription: Use Linq.ofLongs for long-valued data, reducing unnecessary boxing and unboxing in primitive pipelines.
linq.doubleDescription: Use Linq.ofDoubles for filtering, transforming and aggregating double-valued data.
linq.features.filterDescription: Filter elements with where, transform results with select, and control sequence ranges with skip and take.
linq.features.orderDescription: Combine orderBy and thenBy for multi-level sorting, and use groupBy to group elements by key.
linq.features.joinDescription: Correlate sequences with join and groupJoin; use distinct, union, intersect and except for deduplication and set operations.
linq.features.aggregateDescription: Consume results with operators such as count, first and aggregate, or materialize them as lists, arrays and maps.
linq.prepareDescription: The repository README and compiler configuration require JDK 25 or later.
linq.installDescription: Select a build tool and copy the dependency configuration example. Version 1.0.0 is taken from the repository's pom.xml; confirm publication or follow the README to build and install it in a local repository before use.
linq.sampleDescription: Filter even numbers, calculate their squares, and retrieve the query results with toArray.
linq.relatedDescription: Related projects include the Commons Lib utility dependency and the separate linq-in-java repository.

examples.heading: Code examples
examples.runHint: Expand an example to view its complete Java class and output. Configure the dependency, save the code with the displayed filename, and run the main method. After selecting a different dependency version, check its compatibility with the version used by the examples.
examples.source: View this example in the README
examples.commons.intro: This section presents five examples adapted from Quick Examples in the Commons Lib README, with main methods and output statements added. Compilation and output were verified with Commons Lib 1.1.6.
examples.commons.namingDescription: Use StringUtils to convert between snake_case, UpperCamel and lowerCamel naming styles.
examples.commons.intervalDescription: Create a closed-open [1, 10) interval with IntInterval and check its boundaries and formatted representation.
examples.commons.counterDescription: Create a counter with Counter.atomic, increment and add to it, then read its current value.
examples.commons.functionDescription: Calculate volume with TriFunction, using full invocation, partial application and memorized result caching.
examples.commons.pairDescription: Transform the left-hand string with mappedLeft while preserving the right-hand Integer value.
examples.linq.intro: This section presents six queries from the LINQ for Java README, with imports, main methods and required record definitions added. The examples were compiled and run against repository version 1.0.0 with JDK 25. Refer to the dependency section for publication status.
examples.linq.filterDescription: Create an Int sequence with Linq.ofInts, filter even numbers with where, and retrieve the results with toArray.
examples.linq.projectionDescription: Use select and String::length to map names to their string lengths and collect the results into a List.
examples.linq.orderingDescription: Apply multi-level sorting by age and then name. Person.toString retains the README output format; the optional annotation is omitted.
examples.linq.aggregationDescription: Calculate the sum and average with IntEnumerable's sum and average methods. The example corrects the README output label age to avg.
examples.linq.setsDescription: Use distinct, except, intersect and union for unique values, difference, intersection and union.
examples.linq.studentsDescription: Based on the README Student example, select students with scores of at least 80, order by descending score, and extract their names.

chapter00.intro: This chapter covers JDK 25, IntelliJ IDEA and the Fabric template, followed by IDEA settings, the project structure and the References class.
chapter00.baseline: Chinese labels may vary by language pack. Search Settings for the English name when needed.
chapter00.environment.title: Development environment
chapter00.environment.jdkIntro: Download JDK 25 for your operating system and processor architecture.
chapter00.environment.arch: Select x64 for a typical Windows PC or aarch64 for an Apple Silicon Mac. After installation, confirm that both commands report major version 25.
chapter00.environment.jdkMismatch: If the versions differ, check PATH and JAVA_HOME. JAVA_HOME must point to the JDK root.
chapter00.environment.ideaIntro: Open the template project and select JDK 25 for Project SDK and Gradle JVM.
chapter00.environment.ideaRuntime: JetBrains Runtime runs IDEA itself. This section configures the project SDK and Gradle JVM. On macOS, Settings is under the IntelliJ IDEA application menu; the remaining categories are the same.
chapter00.environment.generator: Open the official Fabric template generator
chapter00.environment.templateIntro: Select Minecraft 26.3 and enter the mod name, mod ID and package. Example: Vocabulary Spark / vocabulary-spark / io.github.piscescup.vocabularyspark.
chapter00.environment.templateOptions: Enable split client sources and data generation as needed. Extract the project, open its root directory in IDEA and wait for Gradle sync.
chapter00.environment.firstRun: Run the command for your operating system from the project root:
chapter00.environment.success: A successful client launch verifies the setup. Check Build or terminal errors if it fails.
chapter00.settings.title: IDEA settings
chapter00.settings.intro: The following settings include Chinese and English navigation paths. Appearance options such as theme and font can be adjusted to personal preference. File and console encodings are configured separately.
chapter00.settings.shortcuts: Shortcuts: Ctrl + Alt + S on Windows/Linux; ⌘ + , on macOS.
chapter00.settings.reopenBody: Enable to restore the last projects; disable to show the welcome screen.
chapter00.settings.updatesBody: This stops automatic IDE update checks and notifications. It isn't an installation lock. Plugin updates have a separate option. If IDEA is managed by JetBrains Toolbox, turn off automatic tool updates in Toolbox Settings → Tools → Update all tools automatically; the IDE's update page mainly handles plugins in that setup.
chapter00.settings.themeBody: Sets the application and toolbar theme.
chapter00.settings.uiFontBody: Enable the custom font to adjust menu and project-tree text.
chapter00.settings.backgroundBody: Choose an image and opacity. This project only limits it to the current project.
chapter00.settings.editor: 2.4 Editor colors, font size and comments
chapter00.settings.schemeBody: Sets syntax colors. Duplicate a built-in scheme before editing it.
chapter00.settings.codeFontBody: Sets the font and size. A scheme-specific font overrides this default.
chapter00.settings.commentsBody: Select the comment type and foreground color. For Java-only changes, use Color Scheme → Java and clear Inherit values from if needed.
chapter00.settings.linesBody: Enable line numbers and method separators as needed.
chapter00.settings.completionBody: Enable Show suggestions as you type and adjust Match case. Ctrl + Space triggers completion on Windows.
chapter00.settings.importBody: Enable Add unambiguous imports on the fly; optionally enable Optimize imports on the fly. Check package names when multiple classes share a name.
chapter00.settings.importReminder: Still check the package name. Different Minecraft versions and libraries can contain similarly named types. Match the package used by the example. IDEA needs your choice when more than one candidate fits.
chapter00.settings.encodingBody: Set Global Encoding, Project Encoding and the Properties default to UTF-8. Check directory overrides as well.
chapter00.settings.encodingConvert: For existing files, choose Reload or Convert according to the original encoding. Native-to-ASCII conversion is separate from UTF-8.
chapter00.settings.consoleBody: Select UTF-8. If text is still garbled, also check the program's output encoding.
chapter00.settings.header: 2.10 A header for new Java classes
chapter00.settings.headerBody: Set the file-header template and replace the author name. ${NAME} is replaced with the class name when a file is created.
chapter00.settings.headerScope: Default applies to the IDE; Project applies to the current project. Keep one #parse("File Header.java") in Files → Class. Templates affect new files only.
chapter00.settings.source.header: A header for new Java classes
chapter00.plugins.title: Development plugins
chapter00.plugins.intro: After setting up the environment, install the following plugins as needed. They provide editor assistance; Gradle continues to manage project dependencies.
chapter00.plugins.mcdevBody: Adds Minecraft inspections and navigation. Choose a version compatible with IDEA 2026.3; create the project with Fabric's official generator.
chapter00.plugins.languageBody: Chinese support is bundled. If unavailable, check that Chinese Language Pack is enabled in Plugins → Installed.
chapter00.files.title: Project files
chapter00.files.intro: Gradle configuration defines the build process and dependencies. Fabric configuration describes the mod and its entrypoints. The following files are from the Minecraft 26.3 template.
chapter00.files.gradleRow0: Declares Loom, Minecraft and Fabric dependencies, compilation and resources. The 26.3 template uses net.fabricmc.fabric-loom.
chapter00.files.gradleRow1: Version and project properties: minecraft_version, loader_version, fabric_api_version, version and group.
chapter00.files.gradleRow2: Defines the project name and plugin-resolution repositories.
chapter00.files.gradleRow3: Pins the Gradle version used by the project's wrapper.
chapter00.files.gradleRow4: Wrapper launchers: gradlew for macOS/Linux and gradlew.bat for Windows.
chapter00.files.gradleRow5: Local caches and build output; exclude from source control.
chapter00.files.fabricRow0: Common Java code and the ModInitializer entrypoint. Keep client-only types separate.
chapter00.files.fabricRow1: Client code and ClientModInitializer when split sources are enabled.
chapter00.files.fabricRow2: Declares id, name, version, environment, entrypoints, depends and mixins.
chapter00.files.fabricRow3: Client assets under resources, using the mod ID as namespace.
chapter00.files.fabricRow4: Server data such as recipes and loot tables; create as needed.
chapter00.files.fabricRow5: Mixin configuration; client configuration can live in src/client/resources.
chapter00.files.fabricRow6: Output from data generation. Update the generators and regenerate.
chapter00.files.idReminder: A mod ID can be vocabulary-spark; Java package names cannot contain hyphens.
chapter00.files.buildBody: Artifacts are in build/libs. Distinguish the mod JAR from a sources JAR.
chapter00.habits.title: My development practices
chapter00.habits.intro: I keep the mod ID, metadata, logger and shared helpers in a References class for maintenance.
chapter00.habits.exampleIntro: Add the project's package declaration and keep the mod ID consistent with fabric.mod.json.
chapter00.habits.row0: The mod ID and resource namespace.
chapter00.habits.row2: Looks up the container by ID; orElseThrow() fails if absent.
chapter00.habits.row3: Mod metadata, including the name and version.
chapter00.habits.row4: Shared JSON serializer with pretty printing and HTML escaping disabled.
chapter00.habits.row5: Log4j logger; import the matching Logger type.
chapter00.habits.row6: Adds the mod namespace to a resource path. Pass no namespace prefix.
chapter00.habits.call: Example: creating a texture resource identifier:
chapter00.habits.lifecycleBody: Calling fromPath() also initializes metadata fields, so use it after Fabric has loaded mod metadata. Reading the compile-time constant MOD_ID alone generally does not trigger initialization.
chapter00.habits.constant: MOD_ID is a compile-time String constant, so reading it alone generally doesn't initialize the class. MOD_NAME and MOD_VERSION are runtime fields. If you later want a fully independent ID helper, separate fromPath() from metadata lookup.
chapter00.habits.annotationsBody: JSpecify's @NonNull marks a non-null return type. JetBrains' @Contract("_ -> new") describes a fresh return value. These guide static analysis rather than checking null at runtime.
chapter00.habits.versionBody: MC 26.3 uses net.minecraft.resources.Identifier. This example uses Log4j, while the official template uses SLF4J. Import the matching Logger type.
chapter00.finish.title: Chapter checklist
chapter00.finish.body: Confirm that the development client starts and Gradle builds successfully, and check the file and console encodings. Use the References fields and helpers as needed in later development.
